identity.title: Are VLMs Seeing or Just Saying? Uncovering the Illusion of Visual Re-examination

problem.claim: The paper asks whether VLMs’ self-reflective statements about checking an image correspond to genuine visual re-examination or learned textual patterns.

contributions.claim: Introduces VISUALSWAP, which replaces a reasoned-over image with a visually similar but semantically different image to probe whether the model notices.
Introduces VS-BENCH, a benchmark of 800 image pairs curated from four multimodal-math datasets.
Reports that visual re-examination claims often fail to reflect actual visual re-examination, with distinct vulnerability across model settings and generation behaviors.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present VISUALSWAP and VS-BENCH as their framework and benchmark for probing the gap between reflective language and visual re-examination.

author_reported_evidence.claim: In experiments on Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL, and ERNIE-VL, models overwhelmingly missed image swaps, with accuracy dropping by up to 60%.
The authors report that thinking models were nearly three times more vulnerable than instructed counterparts, while scaling did not mitigate the vulnerability.

Multi-turn user instructions restored visual grounding, whereas self-generated reflective statements during continuous generation did not; the authors associate this with increased attention to visual tokens under user instructions but not self-reflection.

narrative_sequence.summary: VLMs commonly generate statements about checking the figure again, motivating a test of whether those statements reflect actual visual inspection.
VISUALSWAP tests visual re-examination by swapping in a visually similar but semantically different image after initial reasoning.
VS-BENCH provides 800 image pairs drawn from MathVista, MathVerse, MathVision, and MMMU-Pro.
Experiments report widespread swap blindness, greater vulnerability in thinking models, no scaling mitigation, and restoration by user instruction but not self-reflection.
Attention analysis links restored grounding to elevated attention on visual tokens under user instructions, unlike self-reflection.

source_observation.claim: The paper probes reflective claims by changing the visual input while preserving visual similarity and testing whether the model notices.

lessons.interpretation: Counterfactual input changes can distinguish language about a reasoning action from behavior that depends on performing it.
lessons.application: For claims about tool use, retrieval, or re-reading, construct minimally changed inputs that preserve surface form but alter decisive semantics, then test action sensitivity.
lessons.exception: This design is unsuitable when no controlled input substitution can isolate the claimed operation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact evaluation task, baseline accuracies, swap-construction protocol, or statistical details behind the reported 60% drop and nearly 3x vulnerability.
The abstract does not establish whether the reported patterns generalize beyond the named models, datasets, or visual-swap benchmark.
